analysis.one_liner: Closes tax loopholes that let multinational oil companies avoid U.S. tax on foreign profits.
analysis.headline: Referred to the Senate Finance Committee with zero cosponsors; no committee action since introduction, and the session ends in January.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill raises the U.S. tax bill of multinational oil and gas companies on their foreign operations. It ends a special carve-out that currently leaves foreign oil-extraction profits outside the minimum tax the U.S. applies to profits of foreign subsidiaries, adds oil shale and tar sands to the categories of income covered, and stops companies from counting payments to foreign governments as tax credits when those payments buy them something valuable, like the right to drill. The money involved flows to the U.S. Treasury; the bill directs it nowhere specific.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people benefit only indirectly: the federal government would collect more revenue from multinational oil companies, which reduces the burden on everyone else or funds public priorities. Honest U.S. oil and gas producers who already pay full tax could also face slightly fairer competition against rivals that use the loopholes.

how_it_helps.text: Currently, income from foreign oil and gas extraction is carved out of the minimum tax (called GILTI) that applies to U.S. owners of foreign subsidiaries, so those profits can escape the minimum rate entirely. The bill strikes that carve-out, putting oil-extraction income under the same minimum tax as other foreign profits.
The bill expands the definitions of covered oil income to include extraction from oil shale and tar sands, closing a definitional gap in the foreign tax credit rules.

The bill restores "dual capacity taxpayer" rules: a company that pays money to a foreign government and in return receives a specific economic benefit (such as access to oil) cannot count that payment as a foreign tax credit against its U.S. bill. This rule existed before the 2017 tax law repealed it.
The changes apply to tax years starting after enactment (and after December 31, 2026 for the dual-capacity provision), so they would close the loopholes going forward rather than retroactively.

analysis.who_pays: Multinational oil and gas companies with foreign operations, which would pay more U.S. tax on their foreign extraction income. Some of that cost could, at the margin, show up in fuel prices or in returns to shareholders.

drawbacks.text: The bill raises costs for U.S.-based multinational oil companies only; foreign-headquartered rivals do not owe U.S. minimum tax at all, so the change could slightly shift investment toward foreign competitors rather than reduce drilling overall.

Corporate taxes on oil extraction can be passed through to consumers at the margin, so some of the cost could reach households through fuel prices, though the effect would be far smaller than a broad energy tax because it applies only to foreign-source income of U.S.-owned companies.
The bill contains no provision directing the new revenue to any specific purpose, so its benefit to ordinary people is diffuse and depends on how Congress uses the money.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This is a loophole-closing bill: it removes tax breaks that a specific industry won in the 2017 tax law, rather than imposing a broad new tax. The cost is real but narrow — higher taxes on foreign profits of U.S.-owned oil multinationals, some of which may trickle to consumers or shareholders. The benefit to ordinary people is indirect (federal revenue), and the bill is narrowly drawn without any companion use of the money. Honest supporters would acknowledge it is a modest fairness fix, not a sweeping change to energy or tax policy.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in August 2026, read twice, and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has sat without a hearing, markup, or vote while the session runs out.

narrative.text: Senator Heinrich introduced the bill on August 6, 2026.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day.
The bill's only recorded actions since referral are none — the Finance Committee has not scheduled a markup or vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Multinational oil and gas companies keep the carve-out from the foreign-profits minimum tax, the tar sands and shale gap, and the ability to count payments to foreign governments as tax credits. No other group is measurably better off.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Multinational oil companies keep their tax breaks

for.name: Sen. Martin Heinrich
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to close foreign tax loopholes for oil companies; no senator joined him as a cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Has taken no action — no hearing, markup, or vote — since the bill was referred in August 2026, with the session ending January 3, 2027.

against.name: Sen. Mike Crapo
against.what_they_did: As chair, controls the committee's schedule and has not scheduled any consideration of the bill.

sides.party_line_note: No votes ever occurred, so the partisan shape cannot be measured; the only support on record is one Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors of either party.

industries.note: The bill raises their U.S. tax bill on foreign oil income: it removes the exclusion of foreign oil-extraction income from the GILTI minimum tax, adds tar sands and oil shale to covered income, and reinstates rules barring companies that pay foreign governments for special benefits (like drilling access) from claiming those payments as tax credits. These breaks date to the 2017 tax law, so passing the bill would unwind an industry-specific win; ordinary people's stake runs the other way, since the revenue would come out of corporate profits rather than them.

industries.industry: Tar sands and oil shale producers
industries.note: Their extraction income, which currently falls outside the foreign oil income definitions, would become taxable under the same rules, removing a definitional advantage.

analysis.trajectory: The bill is effectively dead for this Congress. It has a single sponsor, zero cosponsors, and sits on a committee calendar controlled by the opposing party's chair, with the session ending in early January 2027. Tax bills of this kind rarely move without either a cosponsor bloc or a budget-reconciliation vehicle, and neither exists here.
